paragraphs: Designing an antibody involves choosing both its amino-acid sequence and its three-dimensional structure. These choices are closely connected in the complementarity-determining regions, or CDRs, at the antibody’s tips. Those regions determine binding specificity between an antibody and an antigen. This paper proposes a hierarchical training paradigm, HTP, to support the joint design of sequence and structure.

HTP organizes training into four stages, each associated with a particular protein modality and domain. Carefully chosen tasks connect geometric graph neural networks, which work with structural information, to large protein language models, which work with sequence information. This lets the approach draw on geometric structures alongside large databases of both antibody and non-antibody sequences, bringing several sources of evolutionary information into the design process.

The reported experiments establish new state-of-the-art performance for joint sequence–structure design and for design with a fixed backbone. The contribution is a training strategy for combining complementary protein information, with empirical evidence that this combination improves the evaluated design tasks.
neurips-2023-a-hierarchical-training-par.tldr: HTP combines structural and sequence models through four training stages to improve antibody sequence–structure co-design.

paragraphs: Policy optimization improves an agent’s decision rule by adjusting its parameters. Popular methods such as TRPO and PPO rely on parameterized policies, but theoretical understanding has been stronger for tabular representations than for more general ones. This paper introduces a mirror-descent framework designed to accommodate general policy parameterizations and provide convergence guarantees in that setting.

The framework uses the choice of a mirror map to determine the resulting policy class. It can recover familiar classes such as softmax policies, while other mirror maps produce new classes. This links the representation of a policy to the optimization framework used to improve it. Within this framework, the authors establish a linear-convergence guarantee for a policy-gradient-based method involving general parameterization.

The paper also analyzes the number of samples needed when policies use shallow neural networks, reporting an improvement over previous best results. Experiments on classic control tasks support the theoretical claims. Together, these results broaden the theoretical footing for parameterized policy optimization while demonstrating a concrete neural-network application.
neurips-2023-a-novel-framework-for-polic.tldr: A mirror-descent framework accommodates general policy parameterizations and establishes linear convergence with improved sample-complexity results for shallow networks.

paragraphs: Vision transformers become expensive when high-resolution images produce long token sequences. This is particularly relevant to dense prediction tasks such as segmentation and object detection. AiluRus starts from the observation that object contours and shapes can matter more for these tasks than texture inside objects, motivating different computational resolutions across an image.

At an intermediate transformer layer, a spatially aware clustering procedure selects anchor tokens. Tokens adjacent to these anchors are merged into lower-resolution regions, while other tokens remain separate. Subsequent layers process the shorter sequence, reducing computation. Before making predictions, the method unfolds merged tokens to restore the feature map’s resolution, connecting the computational savings to the spatial output required by the task.

Across three datasets, the authors report promising results. Segmenter ViT-L achieves a 48% increase in frames per second without fine-tuning while maintaining performance. In a fine-tuning experiment, the method saves 52% of training time and achieves 2.46 times the frames per second with a reported performance drop of 0.09%.
neurips-2023-ailurus-a-scalable-vit-fram.tldr: AiluRus accelerates vision transformers by merging selected image tokens while retaining finer resolution in other regions.

paragraphs: Many language-model applications involve relationships that can be represented as graphs. This paper asks a more explicit question: can a model read a graph described in ordinary language and perform structured operations on it? The authors introduce NLGraph, a benchmark with 29,370 problems spanning eight tasks, from connectivity and shortest paths to maximum flow and graph-neural-network simulation.

Evaluations of GPT-3 and GPT-4 show preliminary graph-reasoning abilities, alongside significant weaknesses. More advanced prompting and examples supplied in context become less helpful as graph problems grow more complex. The models are also brittle when graph and problem settings contain spurious correlations, showing that apparent success can depend on features beyond the intended graph reasoning.

The authors introduce Build-a-Graph Prompting and Algorithmic Prompting as instruction-based ways to improve performance. Reported improvements range from 3.07% to 16.85% across tasks and settings. These gains demonstrate useful room for prompting improvements, while solving the most complicated graph tasks in the benchmark remains an open question.
neurips-2023-can-language-models-solve-g.tldr: NLGraph reveals preliminary but brittle graph reasoning in language models, with targeted prompting improving performance across several settings.

paragraphs: A language model may give plausible explanations about causes without correctly applying formal rules of causal inference. CLadder is designed to examine that distinction. The paper introduces causal inference in natural language as an evaluation task, asking whether models can reason coherently about causal questions whose answers are grounded in a formal system.

The dataset contains 10,000 samples built from causal graphs and three kinds of queries: associational, interventional, and counterfactual. An oracle causal-inference engine first produces symbolic questions and their correct answers. These are then translated into natural language. This construction connects readable questions to formally determined answers, providing a basis for testing reasoning beyond commonsense judgments about what usually causes what.

The authors evaluate multiple language models and introduce CausalCoT, a chain-of-thought prompting strategy tailored to causal inference. They find the task highly challenging and analyze model behavior in depth. The central contribution is an evaluation resource that makes formal causal reasoning accessible through language while preserving a principled source of ground-truth answers.
neurips-2023-cladder-assessing-causal-re.tldr: CLadder tests language models on natural-language causal questions with formally generated answers and finds the task highly challenging.

paragraphs: Success in reinforcement learning can depend on several crucial actions that occur far apart and long before the final reward. Identifying which earlier steps deserve credit is therefore difficult. Contrastive Retrospection, or ConSpec, approaches this problem by looking back at experience to identify a small set of critical steps through offline contrastive learning.

ConSpec learns prototypes representing those steps using a new contrastive loss. When an agent’s current state matches a prototype, ConSpec supplies an intrinsic reward. The method is presented as an addition to any existing reinforcement-learning algorithm. Its central idea is that retrospectively identifying the few steps on which success depends can be easier than predicting eventual reward at every step.

The authors report that the prototypes support rapid identification of critical steps and make those steps interpretable. They also enable out-of-distribution generalization when sensory features change. ConSpec substantially improves learning across a diverse collection of reinforcement-learning tasks, supporting the usefulness of retrospective critical-step identification for credit assignment.
neurips-2023-contrastive-retrospection-h.tldr: ConSpec learns prototypes of critical past states and rewards their recurrence to improve reinforcement-learning credit assignment and generalization.

paragraphs: CORL is an open-source library for research on deep offline reinforcement learning and offline-to-online reinforcement learning. Its contribution combines algorithm implementations with benchmarking and experiment tracking. The library emphasizes a straightforward development experience, making the code behind an algorithm’s measured performance easier for researchers to inspect and use.

Each method is implemented in a separate single file. This organization makes performance-relevant implementation details more visible within the method itself. An experiment-tracking feature records metrics, hyperparameters, dependencies, and other information in the cloud. Together, the code organization and tracking support examining both how an algorithm is implemented and the circumstances under which its results were obtained.

The implementations are benchmarked on commonly used D4RL datasets. The resulting transparent collection of measurements can be reused for evaluation tools such as performance profiles, probability of improvement, and expected online performance. The paper’s emphasis is on providing inspectable implementations and reusable empirical evidence that support more robust evaluation of reinforcement-learning methods.
neurips-2023-corl-research-oriented-deep.tldr: CORL provides benchmarked single-file reinforcement-learning implementations with experiment tracking and reusable evaluation results.

paragraphs: Session-based recommendation predicts an anonymous shopper’s next purchase from their browsing and purchase history. Adding graphs of item transitions can supply context, but those graphs can also introduce noisy associations and obscure the shopper’s intent. This paper proposes FAPAT, a transformer-based method that represents intent through transitions and recurring patterns in item attributes.

FAPAT builds attribute-transition graphs and matches frequent, compact attribute patterns. These patterns act as memory that augments the representation of a session. A gate and a transformer block then combine this information with the rest of the session. The approach gives repeated attribute relationships an explicit role in representing what the user may currently be seeking.

Experiments cover two public benchmarks and 100 million industrial data across three domains. The authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, averaging 4.5% across Hits, NDCG, and MRR. They also assess intent capture through item-attribute prediction and period-item recommendations, extending the evaluation beyond next-item prediction alone.
neurips-2023-enhancing-user-intent-captu.tldr: FAPAT uses recurring item-attribute patterns as memory to improve session recommendations and capture user intent.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends heavily on how training data are augmented. For time series, suitable transformations are difficult to design because the processes generating the observations can be complex and can change over time. This paper proposes an augmentation method intended to connect examples from the same class and organize their learned representations.

The method builds on mixup while accounting for the non-stationary nature of time-series data. It also controls the degree of disruption introduced by augmentation, described by the authors as controlling chaos. The aim is to make the augmented data useful for learning better features while bringing related examples together in the latent space where the model represents them.

The authors evaluate the approach on heart-rate estimation, human-activity recognition, and cardiovascular-disease detection. Across these three tasks, they report improvements over prior work on optimal data generation and established augmentation techniques. These findings support the proposed augmentation strategy across the evaluated applications and connect its treatment of time-series variation to better downstream performance.
neurips-2023-finding-order-in-chaos-a-no.tldr: A mixup-based augmentation method accounts for changing time-series behavior and improves representation learning across three evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty using a distribution over model parameters. Models sampled from the posterior can provide ensemble predictions and estimates of predictive uncertainty. This paper asks how that posterior should account for sharpness: existing inference formulations may produce models in sharp regions because flatness is not explicitly part of their formulation.

The authors develop a sharpness-aware posterior, together with a Bayesian formulation, theoretical analysis, and a variational-inference approach. Their results address both models sampled from this posterior and the optimal approximate posterior used to estimate it. The proposed construction yields better flatness, connecting posterior inference to a property associated with generalization in deep learning.

The theoretical implication for generalization remains qualified: flatter sampled models may generalize better. Experiments provide a separate empirical result. When the sharpness-aware posterior is incorporated into state-of-the-art Bayesian neural networks, the flat-seeking versions outperform their corresponding baselines on all metrics considered. The work therefore combines a posterior-design principle with evidence of benefits in the evaluated models.
neurips-2023-flat-seeking-bayesian-neura.tldr: A sharpness-aware Bayesian posterior produces flatter models and improves the evaluated Bayesian neural networks across the reported metrics.

paragraphs: Self-supervised Siamese networks learn by bringing representations of related views closer together. A central danger is collapse, where the learned representations become degenerate. Contrastive methods counter this by separating negative pairs, but their performance can be sensitive to having fewer negatives. Positive-only methods often instead rely on asymmetry between source and target encoders.

This paper uses that asymmetric architecture to incorporate the idea of contrastive learning implicitly. Its implementation, guided stop-gradient, changes how the learning process uses the source–target arrangement. The contribution connects the motivation behind contrastive learning with the architecture used by positive-only methods, offering a way to address collapse within that setting.

The authors apply guided stop-gradient to SimSiam and BYOL. They report more stable training and better performance for both benchmark algorithms. The resulting methods also work well with small batches and avoid collapse even when the predictor is absent. These findings show that the proposed mechanism can support useful representations under the specific architectural and batch-size variations evaluated.
neurips-2023-implicit-contrastive-repres.tldr: Guided stop-gradient introduces implicit contrastive learning into asymmetric networks, improving SimSiam and BYOL while resisting collapse.

paragraphs: A best-of-both-worlds bandit algorithm aims to perform optimally in both stochastic and adversarial environments. Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, or FTRL, was developed for the adversarial setting, but suitable configurations can also adapt to stochastic problems. Many earlier guarantees depended on there being exactly one optimal arm, restricting their treatment of problems with tied best choices.

This paper removes that uniqueness requirement for a broad family of FTRL regularizers using a new learning-rate schedule. It extends an earlier result that handled multiple optimal arms for one particular regularizer, the one-half Tsallis entropy. The contribution therefore broadens the range of algorithmic choices for which adaptation can be justified without requiring a unique best action.

For some regularizers, the new regret bounds improve on previous results even when the best arm is unique. The authors also apply their analysis to a setting with decoupled exploration and exploitation. Together, the results strengthen theoretical guarantees while demonstrating that the techniques apply beyond the original bandit formulation.
neurips-2023-improved-best-of-both-world.tldr: New FTRL guarantees accommodate multiple optimal arms across a broad family of regularizers and improve some existing regret bounds.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network involves uncertainty about both its graph structure and the parameters describing its conditional probabilities. Earlier GFlowNet approaches targeted the posterior over graph structures alone. This paper proposes JSP-GFN, which uses a single generative flow network to approximate the joint posterior over the graph and its associated parameters.

Sampling proceeds in two phases. First, the model constructs a directed acyclic graph sequentially, adding one edge at a time. Once the structure is complete, it selects parameters for that graph’s conditional probability distributions. This arrangement uses extensions of GFlowNets beyond discrete sample spaces to handle structural and parameter uncertainty within one generative model.

Including parameters directly in the posterior allows more flexibility in the network’s local probability models. The approach can therefore accommodate nonlinear models parameterized by neural networks. Experiments on simulated and real data show an accurate approximation to the joint posterior and favorable comparisons with existing methods, supporting the proposed combination of graph generation and parameter sampling.
neurips-2023-joint-bayesian-inference-of.tldr: JSP-GFN jointly samples Bayesian-network structures and parameters with one GFlowNet, including networks with nonlinear local models.

paragraphs: Scene synthesis can be guided by human motion, room layouts, or spatial graphs. This paper introduces a task that combines text prompts, human motion, and existing objects as conditions for generating a scene. Combining these inputs creates a representation problem: the model must process different kinds of information together in a unified space.

The proposed solution is a multi-conditional diffusion model. Its distinguishing feature is that it explicitly predicts guiding points for the original data distribution, addressing the combination of conditions through an explicit prediction mechanism. The authors also provide theoretical support for the approach. This makes the handling of multiple conditions a central part of the model design.

The reported experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art benchmarks and demonstrate applications to natural scene editing. These results connect the proposed task to a practical use: generating and modifying scenes under several kinds of guidance at once. The paper contributes both the language-driven task formulation and a diffusion-based method for addressing its combined conditions.
neurips-2023-language-driven-scene-synth.tldr: A multi-conditional diffusion model combines language, human motion, and existing objects to generate scenes and support scene editing.

paragraphs: Synthesizing new views on mobile devices is constrained by computation and storage. Volumetric rendering methods can be especially expensive, while neural light fields offer a direct mapping from a represented ray to its pixel color. LightSpeed investigates how choosing the ray representation can make this direct approach more efficient.

The method uses the classic light-slab, or two-plane, representation. The authors find it effective for learning neural light fields, with a lower-dimensional representation that allows the four-dimensional ray space to be learned using feature grids. These grids make training and rendering significantly faster. The representation choice therefore determines whether a faster computational structure can be used.

Although the light-slab representation is mainly designed for frontal views, the paper extends it to non-frontal scenes through a divide-and-conquer strategy. The authors report better rendering quality than prior light-field methods and a substantially better balance between quality and speed. The contribution ties a classical representation to an efficient learned rendering approach suited to mobile constraints.
neurips-2023-lightspeed-light-and-fast-n.tldr: LightSpeed combines a two-plane ray representation with feature grids to improve neural-light-field rendering quality and speed.

paragraphs: Replicable learning asks whether repeated runs can produce the same canonical hypothesis despite receiving different samples from the same unknown distribution. Because this strong requirement is not generally achievable, the paper studies two relaxed notions: list replicability and certificate replicability. Their associated complexities quantify the degree of replicability while sample complexity measures the data needed.

For estimating the biases of d coins to additive error epsilon, the authors construct a list-replicable algorithm with list size d+1 and prove that no smaller list is possible. They also obtain certificate complexity of order log d, up to logarithmic factors. Both constructions use sample complexity of order d squared divided by epsilon squared, again up to logarithmic factors, for constant error probability.

The results extend to PAC learning for classes learnable with d nonadaptive statistical queries, with analogous list and certificate guarantees and dependence on query accuracy. The proofs use geometric partitions to construct rounding schemes and topological lemmas to establish lower bounds, linking achievable replicability to both algorithm design and impossibility results.
neurips-2023-list-and-certificate-comple.tldr: The paper establishes achievable and optimal replicability complexities for coin-bias estimation and extends its constructions to statistical-query learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops an online quantum learning algorithm for zero-sum games. Its main regret guarantee is written as O-tilde(1), where the tilde suppresses logarithmic factors. The guarantee applies under the game setting studied by the authors. The paper also connects this online-learning method to computing an approximate Nash equilibrium for a matrix game.

For an m-by-n zero-sum matrix game, the algorithm computes an epsilon-approximate equilibrium in quantum time O-tilde(sqrt(m+n) / epsilon^2.5). This expression describes how computation scales with game dimensions and requested approximation accuracy. The algorithm accepts standard quantum inputs and returns classical outputs with compact descriptions, making the form of the final answer suitable for end-to-end applications.

Technically, the method builds quantum versions of classical optimistic multiplicative-weight-update algorithms. Its key component is a fast quantum procedure for drawing multiple Gibbs samples. The contribution thus combines an online regret result, an equilibrium-computation guarantee, and a sampling technique that the authors identify as potentially useful in its own right.
neurips-2023-logarithmic-regret-quantum-.tldr: A quantum online-learning algorithm achieves logarithmic-factor regret guarantees and computes approximate zero-sum equilibria using fast Gibbs multi-sampling.

paragraphs: This paper studies global convergence of policy-gradient methods for finite-arm bandits with linear function approximation. Its central finding is that convergence depends on how a representation interacts with the policy-update rule. Approximation error alone does not adequately characterize that interaction, and exact representability of the policy or rewards is not always required.

For natural policy gradient, the authors establish an if-and-only-if condition: projecting the rewards onto the representable space must preserve the optimal action’s rank. This ordering property is not strongly related to approximation error. For standard softmax policy gradient, they give a sufficient condition combining non-domination of the representation with the ability to preserve reward rankings.

These conditions have different logical strengths and apply to different algorithms. They show why judging a representation only by its approximation accuracy can miss what matters for optimization. Experimental results support the theoretical findings. Within the finite-arm, linear-approximation setting studied, the work shifts attention toward action ordering and its compatibility with the chosen update.
neurips-2023-ordering-based-conditions-f.tldr: For finite-arm bandits with linear approximation, action-ordering properties provide algorithm-specific conditions for policy-gradient convergence.

paragraphs: Continuous-control agents can show large swings in performance during learning. This paper examines those swings through the return landscape, which relates a policy to the return it achieves. The authors find that popular reinforcement-learning algorithms pass through noisy neighborhoods where a single parameter update can lead to a wide range of returns.

The analysis treats returns as a distribution, allowing the authors to map regions of policy space that are prone to failure. This reveals an additional dimension of policy quality: the behavior of returns around a policy matters alongside its performance. The landscape also has exploitable structure, because simple paths through parameter space can lead to policies with greater stability.

Building on that finding, the authors develop a distribution-aware procedure that finds such paths and moves away from noisy neighborhoods. They report improved policy robustness through this navigation. The work connects instability during optimization to local landscape structure and uses that connection to inform how agents can be evaluated and improved.
neurips-2023-policy-optimization-in-a-no.tldr: Studying distributions of returns reveals unstable policy neighborhoods and paths that improve continuous-control policy robustness.

paragraphs: A table model that performs well on broad public datasets may not be the best choice for a particular proprietary table. Its usefulness depends on the table’s domain, schema, and data quality. QATCH addresses model selection by generating evaluations for two SQL-centered tasks: question answering and semantic parsing.

Given an input table, QATCH automatically creates a testing checklist tailored to those tasks. A SQL query engine constructs tests with different levels of complexity. Because the tests are generated around the table and queries, the checks can be used across alternative models. This portability supports examining different systems on a common set of table-specific challenges.

The toolbox also introduces performance metrics that work across the two tasks by evaluating model outputs. The authors demonstrate automatic test generation for proprietary datasets and evaluation of models including TAPAS, TAPEX, and ChatGPT. QATCH’s contribution is a practical way to expose strengths and weaknesses on relational tables that were unseen during training.
neurips-2023-qatch-benchmarking-sql-cent.tldr: QATCH automatically generates SQL-driven tests to compare table models on question answering and semantic parsing using users’ own data.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images from text, but creating variations of a real photograph introduces a gap between real and generated images. The authors trace this gap to differences between latent distributions in the relevant diffusion processes. They propose RIVAL, an inference pipeline that generates variations from a single source image.

RIVAL aligns generation with the source image’s inversion chain, the sequence associated with reversing its diffusion process. The paper identifies alignment at each step as essential for high-quality variations. It combines cross-image self-attention injection, which enables feature interaction, with step-wise distribution normalization, which aligns the latent features. These operations work within a diffusion model without further parameter optimization.

Experiments show better semantic similarity and perceptual quality than existing methods. This means the reported variations improve both their relationship to the source image’s content and their visual quality. The authors also describe the pipeline as applicable to other diffusion tasks, including image-conditioned text-to-image generation and stylization.
neurips-2023-real-world-image-variation-.tldr: RIVAL improves real-image variations without further parameter optimization by aligning diffusion generation with the source image’s inversion chain.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks often use a Gaussian distribution to approximate uncertainty over their weights. Actual weight posteriors can depart strongly from a Gaussian shape even locally, weakening empirical performance. This paper proposes an approximate posterior that adapts its shape using a Riemannian metric determined by the gradient of the log posterior.

The resulting Riemannian Laplace approximation directs samples toward weight regions with low negative log posterior. Sampling is implemented by solving a system of ordinary differential equations. The authors use the structure of the metric together with automatic differentiation to make this computation efficient. The approach therefore changes the geometry used by the approximation while retaining a concrete procedure for drawing samples.

Across the evaluated tasks, the method consistently improves on conventional Laplace approximation. The authors also find that it is not overly sensitive to the choice of prior, addressing a practical weakness of the conventional approach. These empirical findings support adapting posterior geometry as a way to improve Bayesian neural-network approximation.
neurips-2023-riemannian-laplace-approxim.tldr: A Riemannian Laplace approximation adapts to posterior shape and empirically improves Bayesian neural-network inference with less prior sensitivity.

paragraphs: Vision-language compositionality benchmarks ask a model to select the correct caption for an image from closely related alternatives. Such tests are meant to examine understanding of how concepts fit together. The authors find significant biases in all the existing benchmarks they examine, severe enough that models without image access outperform state-of-the-art vision-language models.

SugarCrepe addresses this problem by changing how incorrect captions are produced and filtered. It uses large language models to generate fluent, sensible hard negatives instead of relying on rule-based templates. An adversarial refinement mechanism then aims to reduce remaining biases. These design choices target shortcuts in the caption alternatives that could otherwise undermine the intended visual evaluation.

Re-evaluating leading models and proposed compositionality-improvement strategies reveals that earlier gains were substantially overestimated. The result changes how those gains should be interpreted and motivates further work on compositional understanding. SugarCrepe’s central contribution is a benchmark designed to reduce exploitable biases and make evidence of progress more informative.
neurips-2023-sugarcrepe-fixing-hackable-.tldr: SugarCrepe reduces exploitable caption biases and finds that previous gains in vision-language compositionality were substantially overstated.

paragraphs: Zero-shot image classifiers commonly still require a predefined list of categories at test time. That requirement becomes awkward when an image’s semantic context is unknown or changing. This paper introduces Vocabulary-free Image Classification, where the model must assign a category from a broad language-defined space without being given a known vocabulary.

The authors empirically identify an external vision-language database as the most effective way, among the approaches studied, to obtain relevant semantic content. Their training-free method, CaSED, retrieves captions that are semantically similar to the input image. It extracts candidate categories from those captions, then uses the same pretrained vision-language model to select the best-matching candidate.

This two-stage process makes an enormous category space manageable through image-relevant retrieval and selection. Benchmark experiments show CaSED outperforming other complex vision-language frameworks while using far fewer parameters and remaining efficient. The findings support database-assisted category discovery as a practical approach to classification when the category vocabulary is not supplied in advance.
neurips-2023-vocabulary-free-image-class.tldr: CaSED classifies images without a supplied category list by retrieving captions, extracting candidate labels, and ranking them without training.

paragraphs: Segmenting concealed objects is difficult because their appearance closely resembles the surrounding background. Sparse training annotations add another challenge by providing only limited supervision. This paper addresses both problems with a method that combines multi-scale feature grouping and training masks generated using the Segment Anything Model, or SAM.

The feature-grouping module organizes similar features at several granularities and aggregates the results. This encourages coherent segmentation and helps recover complete objects in images containing one or several objects. For supervision, the method uses the available sparse annotations as prompts to SAM, producing segmentation masks that serve as training labels.

Because those generated masks can be poor, the authors add three reliability measures: combining results across multiple augmentations, weighting individual pixels using entropy, and selecting images using entropy. These steps improve the supervision available to the segmentation model. Experiments across several weakly supervised concealed-object segmentation tasks report state-of-the-art performance, supporting the combined treatment of visual ambiguity and sparse labeling.
neurips-2023-weakly-supervised-concealed.tldr: Multi-scale feature grouping and reliability-filtered SAM masks improve concealed-object segmentation from sparse annotations.
